x0: One platform, three applications. Recover, the first, decides the best next life for every asset that comes back. Resolve brings signals, alternatives, constraints and dependencies into one decision flow, prioritises what matters, coordinates actions across teams and systems, and tracks resolution. Reconcile validates commercial and operational evidence across records, identifies mismatches early, and generates evidence-backed proformas before invoices are issued and disputes arise. Let's start with Recover.
x1: We'll sign in as the planner who looks after returns at this site.
x2a: This cycle, sixty-four assets came back for this customer. Our agent has already sorted them, and marked where to start.
x2b: Take this one, a fifty-five kilowatt motor back from a lease. Our agent pulled its owner, grade, certificate and history from the systems that hold them. Nobody keyed any of it in.
x2c: Ask the agent to summarise it, and it keeps facts and predictions apart: grade B from the workshop inspection, and its prediction, thirty to forty months of life left.
x3o: Its journey has ten stages. Our agent ran the first five on its own.
x3s1: Stage one. The lease ended. Our agent read the contract and opened the case.
x3s2: Stage two. Order management authorised the return, and our agent found a customer order that needs this motor.
x3s3: Stage three. The carrier booked the pickup, and our agent tracked it in transit.
x3s4: Stage four. The warehouse received it, and our agent checked that the evidence was complete.
x3b: Stage five. The M R O workshop inspected and graded it. Ask the agent about this stage, and it shows its work: the grade from the workshop system, the certificate from quality, and why that leaves six routes open.
x4a: Stage six is the decision. Our agent built seven possible routes, checked each one for eligibility, and ruled one out before pricing.
x4b: Then it predicted each outcome with its machine-learning models. The recommendation: redeploy against this customer's replacement order. Ninety-six hundred dollars net, forty-eight hundred better than selling it.
x4c: Ask it why, and the agent explains. It saves buying a new motor for that order, the refurbishment is modest, and the certificate covers the full term. On the right, the evidence it used: each figure, the system it came from, and when.
x4d: Now stress it. Put the workshop cost up thirty percent: the agent still ranks redeploy first. Cancel the customer's order, and the agent re-ranks. Selling becomes the better route, and it tells you by how much.
x4e: You see the agent's reasoning, not just its answer. The planner is satisfied, and submits it.
x5: Stage seven is where a second person decides. Our agent drafted the rationale. The approver reads it, checks their limit, and signs. Nothing goes out until a person approves.
x6: Stages eight and nine. Our agent sends the work to the systems that do it: the customer order, the M R O refurbishment work order, the warehouse and the carrier. Each one reports back, and the agent tracks every reference.
x7: Stage ten. Our agent closes the loop: predicted, ninety-six hundred; actual, ninety-two thirty. Ask it what it learned. The biggest difference was in the workshop, a shaft sleeve found worn at strip-down, and it feeds that line back to the model that estimates workshop cost.
x7r: And this is how our agents ran all ten stages, replayed at twice the speed. Five agents, each with a narrow job: gathering evidence, matching demand, preparing the decision, sending the work out, reconciling the result. Every tool call is named and logged. People made the two calls that mattered.
x8a: All of this runs on top of the systems you already have: your E R P, order management, the M R O workshop, warehouse and quality. We don't replace them; we connect to them. This is the Connection Fabric: twenty systems, connected as they are.
x8b: The source map shows how data flows between them. Pick the M R O workshop, and our agent lights up where its data goes: the condition grading and workshop cost models. Pick the E R P, and you see the demand and price paths.
x8b2: Every system reaches one of seven shared models, and from there, the decision. When a feed goes stale, our agent diagnoses it. Here, an expired token on the market price feed, and how to fix it.
x8c: Source tables. Our agent read each system's own tables, as they are, and proposed how they link: twelve links here, each with its evidence. Your team accepts them, or changes them by hand.
x8d: Canonical models. One shared language for an asset, its condition, the demand and the decision. Our agent maps every system's fields into it, so a grade in one system means the same as a grade in another.
x8e: Workflow Studio. The pipelines that bring data in and send approved instructions out. Our agent set these up, and your team approved them before they went live.
x8f: Need a new one? Ask in plain words. Our agent drafts the steps, checks them, and builds it on the canvas.
x8g: Change it the same way. Every five minutes, and flag any unit that fails its bench test. The agent shows the change first, then applies it. A person still publishes it.
x9a: And how do you know it works? Our agent builds this chart from every closed decision. Each dot is one: what it predicted, against what actually happened.
x9b: With each model version, the error comes down, from about eighteen percent to twelve and a half. Ask the agent what changed, and it shows you, version by version.
x10a: So, to sum up. It works wherever assets come back, in any industry. It sits on top of your E R P, your order management and your M R O workshop, and makes better use of what they already know.
x10b: The agents do the groundwork: the evidence, the options, the paperwork. Your people make the decisions. And every decision gets a little better than the last.
